prize_parts.citation: For establishing liquid-liquid phase separation as a physical-chemical principle that organizes the interior of living cells.

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation is a new concept of molecular organisation. Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules behave as liquid droplets, and Rosen showed that multivalent interactions produce sharp phase transitions with predictable thermodynamics. Together they brought polymer physics, phase diagrams and the idea of a critical concentration into cell biology. The idea has since been tested in many systems and many laboratories, and it now frames work on nucleoli, stress granules, transcription and neurodegeneration. Most of the supporting measurements are chemical ones (binding valency, saturation concentration, interfacial and material properties), so the prize would fall squarely within chemistry. I also think it matters that physical chemistry and the chemistry of life are fairly represented next to synthesis and methods.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the functional meaning of many condensates in living cells is still contested. Some in vitro droplets may be artefacts of overexpression or crowding, and it is not always shown that a condensate does something that a stoichiometric complex could not. A second concern is credit. Pappu and Mittag contributed the sequence-encoded driving forces, and the three-person limit leaves them out. Rosen, Hyman and Brangwynne also stand at different points on the path from observation to molecular grammar, so the priority question is not fully settled. As a soft-matter chemist I should be careful not to over-promote my own field.

responses.point: Linke ranks B022 first and argues that condensates are a clear physical-chemical phase transition with broad reach into cell biology, while noting that physiological relevance is still debated and the split between founding observation and molecular grammar is open.
responses.response: I agree on the physics, but I would not let the physics argument carry the prize alone. Phase separation is the easy part to demonstrate, and the open question for the committee is what it explains in vivo. I think the claim holds for the core principle, namely that cells use liquid-like demixing to organise matter. It is weaker for the long tail of reports of condensate function. A citation should therefore credit the principle and stop short of the functional claims. On attribution I would keep Rosen over Pappu, because the multivalent-protein phase diagram is an experimental result with a quantitative thermodynamic interpretation.

responses.point: Aili ranks targeted protein degradation (B068) first as a new, designable pharmacological modality, with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli as the core laureates, and accepts that clinical approval is still pending.
responses.response: I accept that degraders are a real design principle and I ranked B068 seventh only because I judge it more as medicinal chemistry than as a new chemical concept. The attribution problem concerns me more than the timing. Handa and Ito explained the thalidomide molecular-glue mechanism, and Gray and Sakamoto also have strong claims, so any three names would be disputed. I would like to hear whether the committee would treat PROTACs and molecular glues as one achievement or two. If PROTACs and glues are two distinct strands, then the three-person limit works against B068 in a way that it does not against B022.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks energy-landscape theory of protein folding (B027) first, arguing that it is a conceptually original, mature physical account of folding combining Wolynes and Onuchic's theory with Fersht's experiments.
responses.response: I sympathise with this and ranked B027 third for the same reason, since it reduces a messy biological problem to thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. My difficulty is that the 2024 prize on structure prediction and design touched the same territory, and the folding-funnel story is a theoretical framework that has been less directly tested than the condensate work. I would not call B027 weaker in concept, and it is a serious alternative for me. Where I differ from you is that I see B022 as having a more recent experimental base and a larger present influence on how biologists think.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling (B057) first as a general, mature and clearly attributable method used in pharmaceutical chemistry, while noting some may see it as redundant after the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
responses.response: The attribution to Buchwald and Hartwig is cleaner than for B022, and I take the maturity argument seriously. My reservation is that the committee should ask whether B057 adds a new concept or extends an already recognised one. Many members place it in their top two on the strength of its everyday use. I do not dispute that, but I would not equate heavy use with scientific novelty, and the 2010 prize already honoured the same catalytic logic. I am open to a two-part prize that pairs a synthetic method with a physical-chemical concept, provided the union stays within three people.

uncertainties: How much of the condensate literature reflects functional, physiologically relevant phase separation as opposed to in vitro behaviour.
Whether Rosen or Pappu and Mittag should hold the third place, and how to treat priority among the three.
Whether the committee will treat PROTACs and molecular glues as one achievement or two, which changes the credit analysis for B068.
Whether the expert reports will show that ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B054) are best credited to the Vancouver group alone.
statement.conflict_note: I am a Lund colleague of Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and I direct a membrane and lipid research center that overlaps in topic with B054 (ionizable lipid nanoparticles) and, more loosely, with B022. None of the proposed laureates is a collaborator or a current Lund colleague, and no recusal appears necessary from my profile.
